challenges.name: n-plus-one-evidence
challenges.title: Read the N+1 evidence
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the slow "My learning" page: an APM trace next to pg_stat_statements, and the EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the single query that replaced the loop. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
APM trace of one request:

GET /api/me/courses  user_id=4812  status=200  duration=412 ms
  db.query  SELECT course_id FROM enrollments WHERE user_id = $1 ...      3.1 ms  x1
  db.query  SELECT title FROM courses WHERE id = $1                       2.8 ms  x60
  db.query  SELECT count(DISTINCT lesson_id) FROM lesson_progress ...    3.4 ms  x60
  db spans: 121, db time: 376 ms

pg_stat_statements, same hour:
 query                                                  |  calls | mean_exec_time
--------------------------------------------------------+--------+---------------
 SELECT title FROM courses WHERE id = $1                | 912340 |          0.021
 SELECT count(DISTINCT lesson_id) FROM lesson_progress  | 912338 |          0.048
   WHERE user_id = $1 AND course_id = $2 ...            |        |

Statement: "Both per-course queries run in well under 0.1 ms inside PostgreSQL, so the 120 per-course queries cannot explain most of the 412 ms; the time must be spent somewhere else in the request."
questions.explanation: False. mean_exec_time measures only the time PostgreSQL spends executing the statement. The APM span is what the application waits for: taking a connection from the pool, sending the query over the network, parse and bind, executing, and reading the answer back. Here that is about 3 ms per query, almost all of it outside the executor, and it is paid 121 times: 60 x 2.8 ms + 60 x 3.4 ms + 3.1 ms is about 375 ms, the 376 ms of db time in the trace. The common misconception is that a query that is fast in pg_stat_statements is cheap to call. The cost of N+1 is per round trip, and it grows with N.

questions.question:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) of the query that replaced the loop, same learner (60 active enrollments):

Sort  (cost=96.71..96.86 rows=60 width=44) (actual time=0.981..0.986 rows=60 loops=1)
  Sort Key: e.created_at DESC, e.id DESC
  Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 30kB
  ->  GroupAggregate  (cost=91.40..94.94 rows=60 width=44) (actual time=0.402..0.955 rows=60 loops=1)
        Group Key: e.id, c.id
        ->  Sort  (cost=91.40..92.57 rows=468 width=40) (actual time=0.391..0.437 rows=457 loops=1)
              Sort Key: e.id, c.id
              Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 61kB
              ->  Nested Loop Left Join  (cost=0.99..70.55 rows=468 width=40) (actual time=0.031..0.298 rows=457 loops=1)
                    ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.57..37.10 rows=60 width=36) (actual time=0.022..0.121 rows=60 loops=1)
                          ->  Index Scan using enrollments_user_id_course_id_key on enrollments e  (cost=0.29..9.47 rows=62 width=20) (actual time=0.013..0.031 rows=60 loops=1)
                                Index Cond: (user_id = 4812)
                                Filter: (status <> 'cancelled'::text)
                                Rows Removed by Filter: 2
                          ->  Index Scan using courses_pkey on courses c  (cost=0.28..0.45 rows=1 width=24) (actual time=0.001..0.001 rows=1 loops=60)
                                Index Cond: (id = e.course_id)
                    ->  Index Scan using lesson_progress_user_course on lesson_progress lp  (cost=0.42..0.48 rows=8 width=12) (actual time=0.001..0.002 rows=8 loops=60)
                          Index Cond: ((user_id = 4812) AND (course_id = e.course_id))
                          Filter: (completed_at IS NOT NULL)
                          Rows Removed by Filter: 1
Planning Time: 0.388 ms
Execution Time: 1.032 ms

Statement: "The index scan on lesson_progress still runs 60 times (loops=60), but all 60 lookups happen inside this one statement, so the page now pays for one round trip instead of 121."
questions.explanation: True. loops=60 means the inner side of the nested loop was executed once per enrollment row, but that happens inside the executor: each lookup takes about 0.002 ms and no network, pool or driver work sits between them. The whole statement executes in about 1 ms and the application sends it once. The common misconception is to read loops=N in a plan as "still N+1". A nested loop join is often the right plan for a few dozen outer rows; N+1 is about round trips between the application and the database, not about how many times an index is probed.

challenges.name: my-learning-one-query
challenges.title: One query for the "My learning" page
challenges.description: The "My learning" page of CodeDev sends 1 + 2N queries per view: the learner's enrollments, then the title and the finished-lesson count of every course, one query each. Rewrite load_my_courses(db, user_id) so that it calls db.execute exactly once and returns the same rows: one [course_id, title, completed_lessons] per enrollment of the user whose status is not 'cancelled' ('active' and 'completed' count), where completed_lessons is the number of different lessons of that course the user finished (lesson_progress.completed_at not NULL; the same finished lesson can be stored twice, and a course with nothing finished must still appear with 0). Progress of other users and of courses the user is not enrolled in never counts. Order by enrollments.created_at DESC, then enrollments.id DESC. Tables: users(id, email, created_at), courses(id, title, category, created_at), enrollments(id, user_id, course_id, created_at, status) with UNIQUE (user_id, course_id), lesson_progress(user_id, lesson_id, course_id, completed_at). The test runner at the bottom of the file builds an in-memory SQLite database from each test case, passes a connection that counts db.execute calls, and prints {"queries": <calls>, "courses": [[course_id, title, completed_lessons], ...]}. Write SQL that also runs on PostgreSQL (GROUP BY the primary keys you select from; no SQLite-only functions).
hints: Which table decides how many rows the page has: enrollments, courses or lesson_progress? Start the FROM clause there, and ask what happens to a course with no finished lesson when you join the progress rows to it.

Look at three places: the kind of join to lesson_progress (an inner join keeps only courses that have a match), where the completed_at condition sits (in ON it only chooses which progress rows join; in WHERE it also removes the NULL row a LEFT JOIN added), and what COUNT(column) does with a lesson stored twice.

A similar query on other tables: the number of different paid products per customer, keeping customers with none. SELECT cu.id, cu.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.product_id) FROM customers AS cu LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = cu.id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE cu.region = :region GROUP BY cu.id, cu.name ORDER BY cu.signed_up_at DESC, cu.id DESC. The status filter sits in ON, so a customer without paid orders keeps one row of NULLs, and COUNT(DISTINCT o.product_id) skips that NULL and returns 0.

tests.name: Example: one query, newest enrollment first, a course with no finished lesson shows 0
Cancelled enrollments are left out, completed ones stay; opened lessons do not count
A learner with no enrollments gets an empty list from one query
Duplicate progress rows, other users and courses not enrolled in never count
Enrollments created in the same second are ordered by enrollment id, newest id first
Only cancelled enrollments: an empty list, even with finished lessons
Invalid user id (not in users): an empty list from one query
Large: 120 enrollments and about 1,500 progress rows still take one query
